utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Gajic, I was expecting that you give us some update about translation you have received.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The following translations have been uploaded into the e-system, these are documents marked for identification: D326, D335, D334, D327, and D330.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. They will be now received into evidence. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours, everyone. Mr. President, we also have one document, P2862, which was previously marked for identification for translation, and it has been uploaded and we do have the translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: This document will be received into evidence as well. Mr. Gajic, anything else?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. The Defence has uploaded the public versions of the expert reports, expert Ratko Skrbic's report. The 65 ter numbers are 1D114 [as interpreted] and 1D1115. I can see that there is an error in the transcript. The first document's number is 1D1114. The Defence would request that these two documents be on the 65 ter list. These are documents -- these are expert reports or versions of the expert report that are public.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Vanderpuye, are there any objections to add these documents to the 65 ter Defence exhibit list?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Leave is granted to add them to the 65 ter exhibit list. Anything else? The witness should be brought into the courtroom, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Would you please read aloud the affirmation on the card which is shown to you now.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down and make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sir, you are here as a witness, an expert witness for the Defence, and therefore Mr. Tolimir, as the accused, will put first questions to you in his examination-in-chief, then followed by the Prosecutor in his cross-examination. Mr. Tolimir, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. May the outcome of these proceedings be in accordance with the Lord's will and not in accordance with my desires.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Greetings, Mr. Skrbic. I wish you a nice stay here and I wish you all the best for your career. Mr. Skrbic --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir. Mr. Tolimir, we have some problems with the -- yes, it's better that you use this microphone if it's working today. I hope so very much. The Court Usher will assist you to find the correct position.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Please, although we know each other well, you have to tell us your full name for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: My name is Ratko Skrbic, son of Petar Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, could you tell the Chamber what your current position is.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: I am currently involved in research into the Srebrenica phenomenon, and in the last few months I have been working on my expert report that concerns Srebrenica. And I have been working very intensively on that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, thank you. Please tell the Chamber whether you have already testified before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, I have never testified in any of the cases before this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic and Mr. Tolimir, you are using same language and, therefore, please pause between question and answer and try to avoid overlapping. The interpreters wouldn't catch everything what you have to say. Please carry on, Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, please follow the transcript on the screen. When my question is completely transcribed, then you can provide us with your answer.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I've understood that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see 1D103. And let me repeat the number, 1D1039. The previous one was not the correct number. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, we can now see your curriculum vitae. And my question is as follows: Mr. Skrbic, since this is a very brief curriculum, could you provide us with a more precise information that concerns your educational background? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: I finished primary school in the village that I was born in. I completed secondary school in the municipality of Glamoc, which is where I was born. After the secondary school I went to the military academy of the land forces, the centre for nuclear, biological and chemical defence. I then finished the command staff tactical training school in the centre of high military schools within the JNA, and after that I completed a course at the All People's Defence school, it's a war college. It's the highest military college that existed in the army at the time. That is my educational background.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Please tell the Chamber which positions you were able to hold as a result of these -- these schools that you attended.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: After having completed my training at the military academy, I was responsible for performing the duties of a platoon and company commander, and I did so since 1987, since -- from 1979, in fact, until 1984. From 1979 until 1984, I was a instructor in the centre for nuclear, biological and chemical defence. I worked in the tactical department. I instructed on tactical use of nuclear, biological, and chemical defence. That was in all the relevant schools, in the school of the reserve officers, in the military academy and in the secondary military school. Having completed the command staff school for tactics, I was responsible for commanding regiments and for work in the staff organs of operation units. These are corps. Having completed the war school, the war college, I was capable of performing all high military duties in the army, including the Ministry of Defence. I could also perform the duties of chief of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Please tell the Chamber how your career progressed within the service until 1993.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Having completed the military academy, I performed my duties in Krusevac, which is where I completed my military training in the academy. I was a platoon commander from 1973 until 1976 -- I apologise, 1977. And from 1977 until 1979, I was a company commander in Krusevac, a company commander for nuclear, biological, and chemical defence. I was then moved to the tactical department, and I was, in particular, responsible for teaching nuclear, biological, and chemical defence. I held that position until 1984. In 1984 I was transferred to the military technical institute of the land forces, to the Mostar laboratory unit. I was appointed as deputy chief of the institute. I remained in that position until 1988. When I was sent for training in the tactical command school that took up one year. I completed that course, that school, in 1989. And then in 1989, I was sent from the school to the military naval region of the 9th Corps in Knin. I was the chief of nuclear, biological, and chemical defence in the corps command. And the next year, in 1990, I was sent to complete a course in the All People's Defence school. I completed that course in 1991 and again returned to the military technical institute of the land forces, to the Mostar laboratory unit. I remained there until the end of January 1992, which is when the institute was transferred or relocated in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. For the sake of the transcript, which year was it that you returned to Serbia from Mostar?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: That was the end of January 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please slow down a little bit and make a pause after I put a question to you. Mr. Skrbic, when you became -- when did you become a member of the Army of Republika Srpska? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: I became a member of the Army of Republika Srpska on the 8th of February, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell me what establishment position you occupied or what duties you performed in the VRS. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was first appointed as the Chief of Staff in a brigade in the VRS. If necessary, I can give you the name of the brigade. It was the 17th Kljuc Brigade in the 2nd Krajina Corps, and I performed those duties until November 1993. In November 1993 I was appointed as commander of the 15th Bihac Brigade within the 2nd Krajina Corps, and I performed those duties until the end of the conflict in Bosnia-Herzegovina -- or, rather, until the time at which the Dayton Agreement was signed. And then, within a few months, the 2nd Corps was reorganised as well as its component brigades, that also included my brigade. I can't remember the exact date, but towards the end of February or at the beginning of March I was transferred to the Main Staff of the Army of Republika Srpska. That was in 1996. And I was in the sector for moral guidance, religious affairs, and legal affairs. I was an officer for psychological and propaganda activities. I remained in that position for a few months. I wasn't involved in those activities because I was in the team for visiting troops to see how the reorganisation or restructuring of the army was going. Unfortunately, in May of that year, 1996, I fell ill. I had a heart attack. In September I had heart surgery. I then requested a transfer. And in 1997, I was, in fact, transferred to the Army of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: May I --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- interrupt for a moment. Again, please slow down while speaking. You are speaking very fast and it's very difficult for the interpreters to catch everything you are saying. I have one question. When did you enter the JNA first? You didn't provide us with this information.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1969, when I commenced my training in the military academy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Please, could you tell the Chamber which geographical region -- in which geographical region did you perform duties in the 2nd Krajina Corps? We want to see what the relationship was with the Main Staff, because that involves your movement in Republika Srpska. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: I was in Western Bosnia. The area I performed my duties in was the extreme western part of Bosnia at the border with Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was this near the Bihac protected zone?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was close. It was at the edge of the Bihac protected zone.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Was your brigade deployed on the borders of the Bihac protected zone, and were any BH forces in Bihac or was any other unit between you?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, there was no other unit between us. I was in direct combat contact with the forces of the 5th Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, Mr. Skrbic, please, can you tell us something about your career in the Yugoslav Army? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: In 1997, I was transferred to the Yugoslav Army and appointed as the chief of the nuclear, atomic and chemical defence arm within the special unit corps of the Yugoslav Army. I remained in that position until 1999, to be more precise, until March 1999, when the NATO aggression against Yugoslavia commenced. At that time, I was transferred to the 1st Administration of the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army, which is an operational administration. And I spent there the entire period -- or the entire duration of the aggression against Yugoslavia. After that, I was appointed to the General Staff of the Yugoslav Army to its personnel administration as assistant chief of the department of the 30th Personnel Centre, and I discharged those duties until 2001. In 2001, I was appointed to a new position to the department of strategy of the school for national defence within the military academy as the head of the teacher's group for command staff training, and I also provided instruction in the course of that position until I was appointed senior instructor in the next year, which is the position that I held until the 30th of July, 2005, when I retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell us which specific courses you taught in the command staff training school and general staff training school?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: During all post-graduate courses, command staff --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Once again, the interpreters are asking you to slow down. You are very, very fast, and we want to understand your evidence and to have everything on the record. Please speak more slowly. Now continue, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, can you please repeat the last part of your answer because it wasn't recorded, and please slow down.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Can you please remind me what the question was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: The question was which courses you taught in command staff and general staff additional training?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: During all these post-graduate trainings, I taught subjects such as military strategy and warfare.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you tell Chamber what does "warfare" mean in our language?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: That is the art and the skill of waging a war.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since you said that you retired on the 30th of July, 2005, can you tell us whether you were involved in any other work related to the military following your retirement?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, not directly. But in that same year, I started working on the defence team as an investigator, the defence team of General Miletic. If you consider that to be a military-related duty, then I can say yes, I was involved.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please have in e-court document 1D -- actually, I would like to tender that into documents [as interpreted], because we already have it in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Are you tendering 1D1039?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, this document shall be assigned Exhibit D351. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Before we move to another document, I have one additional question to your CV. It's a more personal question. Are there close relatives in your family who were also members of or have been members of the VRS?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't have any close relatives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What about the profession of your father?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My father was a farmer and unfortunately died very young.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. For the purpose of presenting evidence in this case, you provided two expert reports. Can you tell us which specific reports you have prepared?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, the first expert report that I drafted is a report on the movement of the population of Srebrenica, and the other one is entitled: "Srebrenica and Zepa."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court, please, document 1D1114, that's the first report entitled: "The Movement of the Population of Srebrenica." Thank you. My thanks to e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, can you tell us which sources you relied upon when you drafted this report.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: While I was preparing this report, I was using documents of the Army of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, documents of the local political authorities of Srebrenica, documents provided by the United Nations starting from the Secretary-General report attached to various resolutions, as well as reports of commanders and assistant commanders of UNPROFOR units stationed in Zagreb. Then I also used documents of international humanitarian organisations, such as ICRC, UNHCR, and others. And that would be more or less the documents that I relied upon.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you please tell us, tell the Chamber, did you draft this report on your own? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did it completely on my own.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, can you please tell the Trial Chamber whether anyone made any suggestions to you with regard to the conclusions that you arrived at in your report. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. Nobody made any suggestions of that kind, and even if it had been the case, I would have definitely refused that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you please tell us how long you dealt with the issue of the movement of the population of Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Starting from 2005 when I started working as an investigator on the General Miletic's Defence team.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Mr. Skrbic, since you're a military expert, can you explain to us whether military analysts also deal with the issue of movement of populations during wartime and to what end? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, they do. This is studied at the highest-ranking military schools as well, although as a minor subject. The purpose of studying this particular issue is to explore the possibility of recruitment because population is the source of recruitment for other defence elements in an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Can you please explain what you meant by other defence system elements? Because it was not properly recorded in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. It is not only an army that is part of the defence system, there are other organs there as well such as the civilian protection, which includes civilian defence. Then there are work obligation units, and organs of the civilian protection which do not have the status of units but do carry out certain defence operations such as surveillance and alerting the population and giving raid signals to the population in case of a threat.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you tell us, did you have an opportunity during your training to study the methodology of the movement of populations and losses incurred in the course of a war?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I was at the school of All People's Defence, I even remember that one of my colleagues prepared his thesis entitled: "The Assessment of Losses in an Armed Conflict and the Possibility of the Strain Imposed on the Population With a View to Making Up for the Losses Incurred by Units."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please explain the term "losses," what does it imply?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Losses imply any combatant who is out of action, whether due to the fact that he was killed, seriously wounded, or lightly wounded, in which case he is only temporarily out of action but it is, nevertheless, counted as a loss.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you study demographic issues as well or, rather, why a soldier or a military analyst deals with issue pertaining to demographic problems? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: The issue of demographic is very important for the defence system, and that is precisely why it is being studied. Simply because there are areas in every state that are very scarcely populated, whereas, on the other hand, there are regions which are densely populated. This creates a problem from the -- as a -- point of view of defence, which is particularly the case with scarcely populated areas. The highest military commanders and military -- and defence -- Ministry of Defence must take all this into account and must do everything that is in their power during peacetime to bring the regions that were scarcely populated to a normal level by helping the population remain there in order to make it possible for recruiting members of the military from these areas as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Can you please tell us now, what is the goal of your analysis? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: My goal was very simple, and it was self-imposed. I simply wanted to check, I wanted to verify whether the figure of over 7.000 killed militarily able-bodied men who belonged to the 28th Division is correct or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. And I would like to thank the interpreters as well. Mr. Skrbic, and what was your main conclusion? What was the main conclusion you arrived at while dealing with the issues in the report?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: The principle conclusion I arrived at as a result of the analysis -- or, rather, that was demonstrated by the analysis is that the losses of the 28th Division in July and August 1995 could certainly not be expressed in thousands, and the sustainability of the OTP position that over 7.000 men were killed is out of the question. This figure is not sustainable because it cannot be proven in a reliable manner.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. The OTP and the Trial Chamber have certainly read your report on the movement of the population of Srebrenica. We are only going to deal with some of the parts of your report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to call up page 2 in the report. We have it in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: I would kindly ask you, Mr. Skrbic, to explain to all of us what the schematic represents. How did you draw it, based on what information and data?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This schematic represents the schematic of the movement of prisoners from Srebrenica. It was compiled based on the information and data from the statements on the events in Srebrenica or, rather, based on Mr. Butler's expert report. It was also based on the information found in the indictment in this case, as well as on the indictment in IT-05-85-PT [as interpreted], and General Miletic was also included in that indictment, in the indictment in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Do you have anything else to add about this schematic?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, there is.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: I would like to remind everybody, although it's very clearly seen, that different colours were used to represent the different sources of information which served as the basis for the drafting of this schematic. The blue colour represents IT-05-88-PT, whereas the red colour represents the information obtained from the OTP in the indictment that was issued in this case. I did that with an intention to allow everybody to follow the information in parallel and to compare it -- to compare the information from both indictments as well as from Mr. Butler's expert report.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to display page 6 in Serbian, page 5 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, could you please explain the meaning of the table in front of us and what were the sources of information that you used in order to put this table together?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This table is an overview of the capture, detention, and execution of men from Srebrenica. The same sources were used as for the first table that we just saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And can you explain the meaning of the red colour as opposed to the blue colour?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: The red colour represents the information from General Miletic's indictment, and the others are in -- from the indictment in this case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: And what about the black colour? I forgot to ask you about that colour previously. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This is Mr. Butler's narrative.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up page 8 in Serbian and page 7 in English. Thank you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, on this page we see your conclusions under 1, where it says B is bigger than A and C is bigger than B. What is the meaning of these conclusions of yours?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. Firstly, B is greater than A. That means that according to the information found on the schematic, on the two schematics that we have just seen, the number of prisoners transferred who had been soldiers of the 28th Division of the BiH Army is bigger than the number of those who were captured, which is impossible. Only the other way around would be possible. Moreover, this means that B should be less than A by at least 1400 individuals because in the indictment the Prosecutor alleges that immediately after the capture, executions started. And he also mentions very specific places, Cerska, the Jadar River, the Kravica warehouse, and Nova Kasaba. These are the places which are in the territory of Bratunac municipality, places where members of the 28th Division were taken prisoners.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. What you have just told us, would this be found in paragraph under number 1 both in B/C/S and English?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please explain the meaning of paragraph 2, where it says that C is greater than B?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This means that according to the information found in both indictments, the number of executed members of the 28th Division in the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade was greater than the number of those soldiers who had been brought to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade. This is also impossible because it defies logic, it defies natural laws. And if I may continue, please, the purpose of this analysis represented in this way is to show the Trial Chamber that the information regarding the number of detainees, the number of those who were transferred to the area of responsibility of the Zvornik Brigade and executed are not synchronised in the two indictments. They do not coincide. And my conclusion based on that is that the numbers are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we find your conclusions in paragraph 1 and 2 that are now displayed on the screen, on page 7 in English and 8 in Serbian?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up page 10 in Serbian and page 9 in English. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, here we can see another table. Could you please explain what the table represents and what sources of information went into this table? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This table represents an overview of the population of Srebrenica before the 11th of July, 1995. As you can see, the information is relative to January 1994, January 1995, and finally July 1995, which means on the eve of the beginning of combat for Srebrenica. This is also the beginning of my analysis because I decided to follow to the very end the living population. And then based on looking at their numbers before the 11th of July and after the 11th of July, 1995, I wanted to establish whether there was any discrepancy there. The sources of the information in the table for January 1994 is the president of the presidency of Srebrenica municipality. For January 1995, it was the municipal staff of the civilian protection of Srebrenica. And for July 1995, the source was UNHCR and there was also another source, the Dutch Battalion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Since we can see different colours and we also see different figures under the same column, can you explain why that is the case? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Wherever you see a figure in blue, that figure is relative to the number of able-bodied men on a condition that their percentage was 65 per cent and not 60 per cent, as you can see in black. And that percentage is relative to the total number of males in Srebrenica. And if I may continue, please, I did this because I wanted to be scientifically accurate because I was dealing with the percentage of 60 per cent for the year 1981, according to the official statistics, according to the official census. And based on the normal population trends, I introduced the percentage of 65 per cent and that trend was present from 1953 to 1991. I wanted that to account for the increase in the percentage of able-bodied men.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I would like to call up P1806. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, we have a document that you used as a basis for your calculations in front of us. Could you please read it and provide us with the necessary comments.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This is a document from the president of the presidency of the municipality of Srebrenica which he sent to the Institute for Statistics in Tuzla, which is where statistics are in general kept on the size of the population. In this document, he informs the Institute for Statistics on the number of inhabitants in Srebrenica on the 11th of January, 1994. The document quite clearly and precisely shows how many local inhabitants there were and how many of the inhabitants had come from neighboring municipalities at the beginning of the conflict of Bosnia-Herzegovina. They were, in fact, refugees in Srebrenica. At the bottom of the document, the president of the presidency of Srebrenica municipality warns or informs the Institute for Statistics that they are providing them with this information for the purpose of records, but they shouldn't provide international organisations with this information because, as it says here, they are calculating with the number of 45.000 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, unfortunately I don't find this document in the list of exhibits to be used with this witness. Can you help me? Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'll provide you with the relevant number immediately. The expert referred to this document in his report, that's why we included it. We have an identical document, a document whose contents are identical, but the number is different and it was sent in the form of a telegram. We used this one because the witness referred to it in his report, and we didn't want to cause any confusion when following his report, when we, at a later stage, go through that report or read through that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: We are looking forward to receive the other document number. Mr. Tolimir, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. You have now mentioned the warning the president of the presidency of Srebrenica municipality told the Institute for Statistics that they had fewer inhabitants than the number mentioned, and this was done because, as he says here, for the purpose of calculations. Please tell us, what is the difference between this number they have presented for the purpose of certain calculations and the actual number of inhabitants in Srebrenica? The actual number of inhabitants in Srebrenica in January 1994, as it says here.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: The difference is 8.255.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. It was then increased by 8.255. On what basis did you make these calculations? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course, the number is greater than the number of actual inhabitants. And it's a greater number for at least two reasons, in my opinion. The first one is, if you have a larger number of inhabitants, you will receive more humanitarian aid, because, as you can see, he is also warning the institute that international humanitarian organisations should not be provided with the -- this information. The second reason is that, in my opinion, an augmented number could be used to present a more dramatic picture of the humanitarian situation. This could be done by providing information according to which small areas are inhabited by too many people who are not living normal conditions, conditions such as accommodation, work, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. In the document we have, is this an assessment of the number of inhabitants or is it a precise number that reflects the actual number of inhabitants there? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, these are not assessments, estimates. This information is precise information because, as you can see, the document never uses the terms "approximately," or "about," or "more than," and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Please tell us where this augmented information is. Can we see it in this chart or in this schematic -- or, rather, in this document, and if so, where can we find it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can find this information under the title: "Remarks."

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, what is the military significance of such records? Why is it necessary to have precise records pertaining to the inhabitants and who has the responsibility of dealing with such information? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This is a real need and we can link it up to my previous explanation about the reasons for which officers deal with demographic issues and deal with assessing losses sustained. In this particular case, this is necessary to see what the possibilities are to bring up to strength the units of the 28th Division, the units of the civilian protection force, the units that have work obligations to perform. It's also necessary so that we can -- one can determine the number of employees who are needed to work in the companies that were in a position to operate at the time. Such information is necessary, above all, for the Ministry of Defence and for their regional secretariats. In this particular case, the Tuzla regional secretariat of the Ministry of Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Earlier on you said that the difference in relation to the real information was 8.255, and under "Remark," we have the fictional, the imaginary information. Please, we haven't examined these matters in detail, so could you please tell us on what basis do you draw such a conclusion? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: When we have a look at the number of inhabitants in this document, the number referred to before the remarks, the number we obtain is 37.255. And when we take that number away, we deduct that number from 45.000, in fact, we obtain the number I have already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic, for informing us about that difference. You said that in your -- you told us about the purpose of this calculation and the president of the municipality informed -- or, rather, warned the Institute of Statistics. You told us what the reason for this was. In addition to these humanitarian reasons, could you tell us whether this difference is one that is calculated when presenting the numbers of the individuals who disappeared without a trace?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, but in order to be consistent, I also calculated on the base of this number of 45.000, made calculations on the basis of the figure of 45.000.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see D117 in the e-court system. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the document that we still have in front of us is, in terms of content at least, identical to document D116 [Realtime transcript read in error "D1116"].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Nevertheless, it would always be appreciated if you would include into the list of documents to be used with the witness the number of that document which you intend to use. Mr. Gajic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Absolutely, Your Honour. But it's not D1116. I would just like to make this correction, the number of the document is D116. And we now have D117 on the screen. I am saying that for the sake of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Since we have D117 in front of us, Mr. Skrbic, could you please tell us what kind of document it is? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This document was sent by the civilian protection municipal staff. It concerns the number of inhabitants in Srebrenica in January 1995. I'd like to point out that the information contained in this document is even more precise than the information that we saw in the previous document, and it almost conforms to the standards of the regular census that is taken in peacetime conditions because, as you can see, the breakdown includes inhabitants according to their age, their sex, the municipalities that they inhabit, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you tell us why this is of significance for the army? Why is it important for the army that such gender-based information is provided?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: The median value of the number of males and females, or the median value, is about 55 per cent. So the army needs this for the same reasons as in the case of the previous document. They need such information so that they can see what the possibilities are when it comes to replacing losses that are usually sustained in the course of armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. If we compare document P1806 and D117, what sort of conclusions can we draw? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we please see P1806 and D117 on the screen so that we can compare the two documents. D117 so that the witness could answer the question put to him. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to inform the Chamber that when you first have a look at the documents, it seems that the number of inhabitants in Srebrenica in January 1995 is lower that the number of inhabitants in January 1995 [as interpreted]. And that is quite logical for a number of reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, may I interrupt you. This is very unclear and we would like to know your opinion clearly. It is recorded that you have said: "The number of inhabitants in Srebrenica in January 1995 is lower than the number of inhabitants in January 1995." The same time.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness said lower than in January 1994.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Lower than in January 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you very much for this clarification. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that was quite logical for two reasons. The first one is that the inhabitants of Srebrenica left the Srebrenica enclave of their own free will, that included members of the 28th Division and the civilian population. This can be confirmed in documents -- by looking at documents D61, D144, P1807, P988, and D100. In these documents you can quite clearly see in reports from the units sent to the command of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH that the Srebrenica enclave is being left even by members of the 28th Division. They are doing this on their own initiative without any authorisation having been obtained. For example, in document P1807, one can see that in one week alone 1.200 individuals left the enclave on their own initiative. The second reason why we have a lower number of inhabitants in 1995 compared to 1994 is the result of losses during armed conflict; however, this number is much smaller than the number of those who left the enclave.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have D61 and D27 in e-court. I apologise, D61, dated the 27th May. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, can you tell us is that one of the documents that you relied on in order to prove that large numbers of people departed from Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. This is an order issued by Major Becirovic, the Chief of Staff of the 28th Division, whereby he is ordering his subordinate units to prevent any wilful abandonment of the enclave at any cost. And that particularly pertained to military personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. In your opinion, what was the purpose of issuing an order banning anyone from leaving the enclave, especially in view of the persons that this order relates to? Thank you. This document is dated the 27th of May, 1995.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: The first reason to impose this ban was to prevent the weakening of the combat capacity of the 28th Division. And the second reason is that that was a time when the 28th Division was actively involved in combat operations launched from the enclave and when direct preparations were underway for offensive operations in a co-ordinated action with the forces of the 2nd Corps on the front with a view to linking up the territories of the enclaves with the Tuzla district.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: It's now the time of our first break. We will resume at quarter past 4.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I would like to see D116. That is the number Mr. Gajic has provided us with. My problem is that I don't find this number in the list of Defence exhibits, either.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I be of assistance?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: No. At the moment I am only dealing with a document number. Mr. Gajic, shall I take it that this is a duplicate of P1806; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it's not a duplicate in the proper sense of the word. This is an identical wording of the document. The text is identical, whereas the format of the document is different. The first one has a signature, whereas the second one was something obviously sent through packet communications or in the form of a cable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. And both documents are missing on your list. Mr. Tolimir, please -- oh, Mr. Gajic, do you want to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. GAJIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Obviously, our error if it is missing from the list, and we do apologise for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Tolimir, please continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. We saw document D61. Can we please have it briefly they e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, if you look at the last paragraph of this document, i.e., the order of the 28th Division signed by Major Becirovic, it reads as follows: "Any violation of this order by army members will be punished in accordance with the laws in force. I hereby make unit commanders responsible for the implementation of this order." Please, can you tell us what kind of punishment could be imposed on army members in the event of their leaving without permission? And I am referring to the punishment referred to by Major Becirovic in his order.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to note that the date of this document points to the fact that Major Becirovic was, in fact, discharging the duty of a brigade commander, although he has signed himself as the Chief of Staff and he wasn't appointed commander, in fact. I am saying this because it was a well-known fact at the time that the division commander, Naser Oric, wasn't at his command post at the time. He was absent. In fact, he was in Tuzla. As for the punishment that Major Becirovic is making reference to, I have to say that desertion during an armed conflict or during a war is one of the most serious criminal offences that a soldier may commit. And when I say "soldier," I mean both the commissioned, non-commissioned officers, and privates. And if a Supreme Command declares a state of war, and if desertions occur during a state of war, it is possible to impose the most severe sanctions, including death penalty.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Are there any other sanctions that are applicable to deserters apart from death penalty?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Of course there are. I said that that was the ultimate measure, and, of course, everything depends on the legislature of the particular country where the soldier comitted the crime. Other penalties that may be imposed are for the soldier to be stripped of all his rights and benefits that he and his family are entitled to because he deserted from his unit. It is also possible for him to be sentenced to a prison term or to be subject to any other measure.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have in e-court Exhibit P144 [as interpreted]. Thank you. Can we please have D144 in e-court. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, this is another document of the BH Army, the 28th Division command, dated 21st of June, 1995. It is signed, again, by Mr. Ramiz Becirovic, the standing commander, and I am interested in paragraph one, which reads: "The problem of ..." Let's go back to paragraph one. Thank you. "The problem of members of the Army of the Republic of BH and civilians leaving the Srebrenica and Zepa safe area in the direction of Tuzla, Kladanj, and Serbia, has been present since the first days of demilitarisation of this area. During this entire period, the military and civilian authorities in Srebrenica have taken a number of measures to prevent such departures, yet all of these measures have not yielded significant practical results. The reason is that these departures are planned by small groups which carry out the organisation, and it is difficult to uncover them through intelligence work. Naturally, a certain number of people are aware of the intentions of individuals and groups who are preparing to leave, but in general, they show solidarity with them and, following a policy of noninterference, are unwilling to provide information about such people. Sometimes it is possible to uncover and prevent these groups in their attempt to leave the safe area, and we have taken disciplinary measures against them and sentenced them to disciplinary military detention. "For all those who complain of a lack of food and for that reason intend to leave these areas, we have found possibilities for providing assistance in this regard. However, in the summer months, it is as if some unknown wave flows through the people suddenly creating a euphoria that the best solution is to leave for Tuzla. This literally causes waves throughout the entire area, and the majority of people are then ready to leave. Such has been the case in recent days." As we can see, this is dated the 19th of June, 1995. Mr. Skrbic, did you take this document into account as well when you dealt with the issue of the decrease in number of inhabitants of Srebrenica? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is yet another proof that people were -- left the enclaves of their own volition.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Now, please, according to your knowledge, during which periods did the army encounter the most severe problems of desertion?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: That happened most frequently when they found out that fierce fighting was impending, that were planned either by their own command involving their own units, or if they found out about the intentions of the adversary; in other words, if there is a prospect of the most fierce fighting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And in this case why did the population leave the area? Did you find it in the documents? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: In this case, the population of both Srebrenica and Zepa enclaves left the enclaves of their own will. Because they had been an enclave for a long time, they were encircled by the territory of the Republika Srpska. They wanted to put an end to such a life and they wanted to go to safer areas, as they, themselves, called the area of Tuzla, because that's where they saw opportunities for themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And during the period surrounding the 21st of June, 1995, could some military activities also influence such developments in the protected area and outside of it?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes. During that period, the major spring offensive by the BiH Army had already been underway in several directions in the territory of Republika Srpska, including the axis from Tuzla leading towards the enclaves. During that period, the BiH Army had planned to mount a joint offensive by the units in the enclave and outside of it in order to liberate, as they put it themselves, the enclaves and join them up with the region of Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please explain the term "mounting an attack from the front line," what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Combat activities of the 2nd Corps on the front line implied their focal activity from Tuzla in the direction of the enclaves. This also implied the use of forces stronger than those in the enclave. The troops of the 28th Division in the enclaves should have served as the rear forces, behind the enemy lines. The most appropriate explanation would be to see them as landing forces because they had a potential and they always represented a risk for the commander behind whose lines they are deployed. The main body of the forces mount an attack on the front line, whereas the forces in the enclaves would facilitate the efforts of the main body of the forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Aleksandar, for keeping an eye on me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, why were drastic or rigorous measures taken in Srebrenica in order to prevent desertion in view of the fact that people from one territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina wanted to go and settle in another territory under the control of the BiH Army, i.e., Tuzla? Why were such attempts by both civilians and soldiers to desert the area seriously prevented?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: It would be rational to conclude that the BiH Army, at that time, needed the 28th Division to act from behind the enemy lines. And that is why measures were taken in order to prevent any attempts of desertion.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now I'd like to call up 1 -- P1114 [as interpreted].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Could you please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I'll repeat the number. 1D1114. Thank you. Thank you. I am interested in page 15 in Serbian and page 13 in English. This is the witness's expert report about the movement of the population of Srebrenica. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Here we see another table. Mr. Skrbic, could you please tell us what the table represents and what sources did you use in order to compile the table? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This table represents an overview of the population of Srebrenica after the 11th of July, 1995. They were recorded as refugees in Tuzla and around Tuzla. The sources that I used can be seen in the table itself. The first one was a report by the World Health Organization, the ICRC, the Special Rapporteur on Human Rights. This was taken over from the debriefing, which is a document that was based on a report by the Dutch government, the International Committee of the Red Cross, and the UNHCR. These are the sources of information that was used to compile this table. This table represents the population that left the enclave of Srebrenica after the 11th of July, and it represents all the surviving population.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. And now you don't mention that some of the information was taken from the BiH Army. Please look at line D. There is a figure in red and another figure in black. And then under the source of information in a green colour, we can see Chief of Staff of the BiH Army, General Delic. What does this mean?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I failed to mention that. This is the number of soldiers of the 28th Division who managed to break through. According to General Delic, they were unscathed, by and large, and they were immediately incorporated into the 2nd Corps of the BiH Army. General Delic stated that in the parliament of the Federation of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Just for the record, can you tell us what the number was?

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And now can we see page 21 in Serbian and page 18 in English. Thank you. I would like to thank the e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, please look at the schematic that you, yourself, drafted on the pages that I have just called up, and can you explain the meaning of the schematic and what were the sources of information that helped you to compile it? As well as anything else that may be of benefit for the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This schematic represents a supplement to the schematic of the movement of the population of Srebrenica, which can be seen in the report based on the debriefing. I supplemented that schematic with an intention to provide a clearer view of all the things that are not contained in the previous schematic. One of the things is the horizontal arrow with the figure 10.632 above it. This you cannot find on the schematic based on the debriefing. It is obvious that this figure is correct and accurate because we can see in this schematic how the population of Srebrenica moved. They were split into two groups. One group was composed of women, children, and the elderly. There were 25.000 of them. That group went to Potocari first and from there they were evacuated. The second group, on the left-hand side, was comprised of the soldiers of the 28th Division and other able-bodied males, some 10- to 15.000 of them. They started breaking through towards Tuzla. They separated from their families, and they started a breakthrough towards Tuzla. Here we can also see that in Tuzla, a total of 35.632 refugees were registered. And if we subtract the number of 35.632 from 20.000 that were evacuated, we will end with the number that you can see here, which means that so many able-bodied men had joined the women, the children, and the elderly in Tuzla. And that's how 35.632 refugees were registered. As one can conclude, that figure applies to civilians only. If we continue following the left-hand side of the schematic, we will see that the soldiers continued and that 3.000 of them - and that information was taken from the ICRC - and what you see in the brackets, 5.000, is the number based on General Delic's statement in the parliament, and they joined the 2nd Corps. They were not recorded among the 35.632 refugees. Furthermore, as you can see in the schematic, that means that the figure of 35.632 civilians should be supplemented by the soldiers who had managed to breakthrough, the 3.000 of them or 5.000 of them. In order to respect the principle of consistency, I did my calculations with both figures, and then what we see at the end is that a total of 38.632 people left Srebrenica, or, perhaps, 40.632, if we are calculating on the basis of 5.000. And then in the upper right-hand side of the schematic we can see the figure of 1.000. That's the population of Srebrenica who left and went to Zepa. And if we add the 1.000 to the previous number, we will end up with the number of 39.632 or 41.632. The discrepancy is due to the fact that we started with two different number of soldiers; the first one is based on the ICRC data, and the second one, 5.000, is based on General Delic's statement. If we continue to follow the schematic, we will see that the 39.632 or 41.632 refugees is less than the number of the inhabitants who were in Srebrenica before the 11th of July, according to the Dutch Battalion data. And we will also see that that figure is higher that the number of the inhabitants who were found in Srebrenica before the 11th of July, according to UNHCR data, and that it is more than 42.000, which is the figure that most commonly appears in various documents when discussing the number of the population in Srebrenica at the moment when fighting for Srebrenica started. Furthermore, that means, as you can see at the very bottom of this schematic, that if we took into account the 42.000 people, according to the Dutch Battalion data, and if we subtract 41.632 from that figure, we will end up 368. That could be the discrepancy or the negative number that appears, and one could consider that number to represent those who were killed or went missing or so on and so forth. And finally, according to a different methodology, if we look at the figure 10.632 who joined women, children, and the elderly in Tuzla, and those were able-bodied men, and if we add 3.000 soldiers to them, and they were not registered among the civilians, we will end up with 15.632, i.e., 13.632 to 15.632. I hope that it is not in dispute that all these are able-bodied men fit for military service. That's why I have shown them separately. And I focussed my attention on this particular category because this is category that is most commonly the subject of charges against the Army of Republika Srpska for having lost count of the people in this group of the population. We will see that the figure 13.632 able-bodied survivors who arrived in Tuzla is higher than the lower border of those who started breaking through and that 15.632 is based on General Delic's statement about 5.000 able-bodied men. Then that figure is even higher than the top figure of those who started the breakthrough. You will admit that it is impossible, but the mathematics speak for themselves. And if we take into account 15.000, we will see a discrepancy of 1.368, which means that the figure of over 7.000 killed men cannot persist as the correct number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic --

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: -- I would like to ask you for one clarification. On page 38 of today's transcript, lines 9, 10, and 11, I quote to you: "And we will also see that the figure is higher than the number of inhabitants who were found in Srebrenica before the 11th of July." What do you mean by "before the 11th of July"? To which time-period are you referring?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I say "before the 11th of July, 1995," and "after the 11th of July, 1995," what I have in mind is that before the 11th of July, before the fall of Srebrenica, or before Srebrenica was taken -- well, that's the period I have in mind. And "after the 11th of July" means that I am following the movements of the population after Srebrenica had been taken or, rather, after the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am asking this question. We have seen this morning or this afternoon two documents dated from January 1994 and January 1995. And when you say "before the 11th," to which exact time-period or date are you referring, and what is the source of your information about that number?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am -- really do apologise. I didn't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Then I repeat again. You said: "We will also see that the figure is higher than the number of inhabitants who were found in Srebrenica before the 11th of July." What is your source of information about the number of inhabitants in Srebrenica before the 11th? And now, please, give us a date, the 10th of July, or June, or January, or the January of the previous year, 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was immediately prior to the fighting on the 6th of July, the fighting for Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: What figures of the number of inhabitants in Srebrenica are available for you to that date, and what is the source of it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We saw the figures in the previous diagrams and also in this diagram that I still have in front of me. We can see that these are UNHCR figures, figures from the Dutch Battalion, and the 40.000 figure is one that one can find in document 01007053.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Sorry, sir. You are not answering my question. I am just referring to that sentence you have put on the record. To which time before the 11th of July, 1995, are you referring if you make this comparison to the time after this day? Which time-period?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was in the month of July up until the 11th of July. That was the period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: And you have data from UNHCR and from the Dutch Battalion, specifically to this time-period, beginning of July, yes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I am quite sure that Mr. Tolimir will have the opportunity to show these data sources to the Chamber. Mr. Tolimir, please carry on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, please, when you refer to dates please provide the year on such occasions. And my second question is as follows, it relates to this diagram here. It says Srebrenica, 1.000, arrow, Zepa. Did you make this entry or someone else?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: No, I transferred this from a diagram from the debriefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: In the debriefing is there information according to which a thousand inhabitants from Srebrenica went to Zepa and to Serbia? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: If we go down a bit, the first vertical line under Srebrenica is what I am interested in. It says Kladanj, 10.632; Tuzla -- Kladanj, Gracanica. Did you mark this figure on the basis of your own information or did someone else enter this number here? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: I entered the number.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can this number be found in documents anywhere, this number of 10.632 that left Kladanj and Gracanica and went to Tuzla? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: I didn't find this in any documents. I obtained this number because I found the difference between 31.000 -- 35.632 and 25.000. I calculated the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. And what is this number, Tuzla 35.632, 35.632? Thank you. Where can it be found?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This number can be found in the diagram in the debriefing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Mr. Skrbic, please, in your report, with regard to the movement of 10- to 15.000 people from Srebrenica to Kladanj, well, you call this movement of these people a breakthrough. My question is as follows: What does a breakthrough mean when used in a military sense? What sort of a military term is this? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: It's a combat operation of units that are encircled. Whether this was done on purpose or not. Mostly, it is of a tactical significance and its objective is to allow the unit to break through the encirclement by using the shortest route to reach its units at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Could you please tell us, in this particular case, the breakthrough was made in order to reach which units in which locations, in which region? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: In this particular case, the breakthrough of the 28th Division was carried out in the direction of Tuzla to reach the other units of the 2nd Tuzla Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Could you please tell us how complex such a breakthrough is? Is this a very complex military operation? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Nothing is more difficult than to break through one's encirclement. Units that have been encircled have only two options: Either to break through at great risk to life, or not to break through, not to put up resistance but to surrender and to survive.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Skrbic, according to your analysis, this column breaking through from Srebrenica, from Susanj, Javic [as interpreted], to the territory under the ABiH control, well, is this a typical breakthrough operation or are we dealing with something else?

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: This operation is a typical one. It's a textbook example carried out according to the usual principles that govern breakthroughs. At the head there are brigades or, rather, an armed unit whose task was to break through the encirclement so that the rest of the division could get through. At the tail, there was an armed unit as well. Its purpose was to protect the tail, the rear. And in the middle of the column, some of the soldiers were armed but the majority were men fit for military service who were not armed. That means that the rules and principles governing a breakthrough were respected, and that was in accordance with the possibilities at the disposal of the 28th Division at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Please, could you tell us what the expectations were of those who were leading the unit in the breakthrough and of those who participated in the breakthrough itself? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: The expectation was for them to break through and reach territory under the control of the 2nd Corps of the ABiH. If they hadn't had any such expectations, they would not have decided to pursue such a breakthrough.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Does this mean that a general decision was taken about breaking through, since such a large number actually proceeded to break through? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you. Can a military unit attempt a breakthrough without a decision from the top of the chain of command? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: No. According to military principles in place, according to the prevailing military doctrine, a unit can break through only having obtained authorisation from its superior command and in accordance with its plans. There are certain situations when at the command level a decision is taken to leave a unit within the encirclement and, of course, these situations aren't frequently encountered. But according to the principles governing the military profession, according to military doctrine, a unit can commence a breakthrough having obtained authorisation from its superiors, and it can do so together with other units if the decision and authorisation is obtained at the level of their superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic. Mr. Skrbic, could you please tell us what someone who takes a decision on pursuing a breakthrough has to take into account? What does someone who decides to participate in a breakthrough have to take into account? What sort of things do they have to expect? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: RATKO SKRBIC
utterances.text: Above all, it is necessary to bear in mind the situation. You have to take into account the fact that the enemy will try to prevent a breakthrough from being carried out at all costs. You have to take into account the possibility of carrying out the breakthrough. Secondly, you have to take into account the possibility of sustaining significant losses, because a breakthrough is a military operation that is one of the most risky military operations. In this particular case, the breakthrough of the 28th Division was carried out under very unfavourable conditions, in a tactical sense, in terms of equipment, intelligence that was available, et cetera, et cetera. As a result, the division command, having taken the decision to breakthrough, reached an agreement with the civilian authorities, the local civilian authorities, and they had to expect significant losses because they had to take control of territory that was under the control of the VRS. And the stretch of territory concerned was a stretch of territory 60 kilometres long. In addition, they had to take into account the prevailing situation and the fact that they might find themselves in a situation in which the VRS - provided it managed to block the breakthrough - the VRS could then capture them and disarm them. Or they had to take into account the possibility of continuing with their fight and losing their lives.

utterances.speaker: MR. TOLIMIR
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Skrbic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now have in e-court --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tolimir, sorry for interrupting you. I would like to put a question in relation to the schematic we have still on the screen in front of us. First, I take you back to an answer you provided me with. You said, this is page 42, line 15: "This number can be found in the diagram in the debriefing." Could you please explain what you mean by "debriefing"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't say "reporting." I said "debriefing." And it's a report that was based on the debriefing provided by the Dutch government.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Indeed. And I said "debriefing," and I wanted to get an explanation from you what kind of debriefing you are referring to. What do you mean by that? We all have to understand what you are meaning by using these words. And especially where can be found in your report a reference to this so-called debriefing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The debriefing means research and exploration of the events in and around Srebrenica after they had happened by interrogating soldiers from the DutchBat who returned to the Netherlands. And this had to be done because it is common knowledge that the Dutch prime minister was deposed as a result of these events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Where can that be found in your written report, Mr. Skrbic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You mean where the debriefing can be found, or?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You are referring to this debriefing. I have my own understanding of that, but this is not relevant. I want to know from you where we can find this information in your report which should be the basis of this sketch we have had in front of us. I would like to see the relation between the debriefing and your result. In your report, where can I find it?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps I can be of some assistance.
